items.title: Formula Sheets
items.text:
In studying for exams, I have always known I was prepared once I was happy with my formula sheet. Fortunately, I leared about \(\LaTeX\) early on (i.e., Sophomore Dynamics), and prepping a formula sheet felt the perfect time to learn. Since then, my typesetting abilities have grown with every formula sheet I made; a skill that I deeply value.

So here is a sampling of what I've done over the years! They are presented roughly in chronological order. Although some of the graphics were made by me, there are also screenshots from textbooks as well (e.g., the many tables in Heat Transfer), for which I claim no credit. I do, however, claim credit for every falsehood and typo included.

items.title: Rotation Visualizer
items.text: Rotation matrices are used throughout robotics and dynamics. Sometimes they can be easily imagined, but other times there's simply too much going on. I built this to avoid pulling out a piece of paper everytime.

items.title: The Code
items.text:
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

def vector_rotation_visualizer(rotation, pre_vector=None):
    '''
    Generates a figure to visualize/check a rotation is behaving properly.
    '''

    fig = plt.figure()
    ax = fig.add_subplot(projection='3d')
    fig.set_size_inches(7,6)
    plt.subplots_adjust(left=0.08, right=0.7)

    color_vec = ['r','g','b']
    axis_vec = [r"$x$", r"$y$", r"$z$"]
    for axis_ind, fixed_axis in enumerate(np.identity(3)):
        c_now = color_vec[axis_ind]
        label_now = axis_vec[axis_ind] + r"$_0$"
        ax.quiver(0,0,0, fixed_axis[0], fixed_axis[1], fixed_axis[2],
                    color=c_now, linestyle='dashed', alpha=0.5, label=label_now)

    # Separated for legend sequencing
    for axis_ind, fixed_axis in enumerate(np.identity(3)):
        c_now = color_vec[axis_ind]
        rotated = 0.67*rotation@fixed_axis
        label_now = axis_vec[axis_ind] + r"$'$"
        ax.quiver(0,0,0, rotated[0], rotated[1], rotated[2],
                    color=c_now, linewidth=2, label=label_now)

    if not(pre_vector is None):
        pre_vector /= np.linalg.norm(pre_vector)
        ax.quiver(0,0,0, pre_vector[0], pre_vector[1], pre_vector[2],
                    color='k', linestyle='dashed', alpha=0.5, label=r"$v_0$")
        rotated = 0.33*rotation@pre_vector
        ax.quiver(0,0,0, rotated[0], rotated[1], rotated[2],
                    color='k', linewidth=2, label=r"$v'$")


    ax.set_xlabel(r"$x$", labelpad=20)
    ax.set_ylabel(r"$y$", labelpad=20)
    ax.set_zlabel(r"$z$", labelpad=20)
    ax.set_xlim([-1,1])
    ax.set_ylim([-1,1])
    ax.set_zlim([-1,1])
    tick_vals = [-1,0,1]
    tick_labels = ['{:d}'.format(x) for x in tick_vals]
    ax.xaxis.set_ticks(tick_vals)
    ax.yaxis.set_ticks(tick_vals)
    ax.zaxis.set_ticks(tick_vals)
    ax.set_xticklabels(tick_labels)
    ax.set_yticklabels(tick_labels)
    ax.set_zticklabels(tick_labels)
    ax.legend(loc="center left", bbox_to_anchor=[1.15,0.5])
    ax.set_aspect('equal')
    fig.suptitle("Rotation from dashed to solid,\n lengths are for clarity, and \n do not impart information")
    plt.show()

items.text:
Consider the following, where rotation \(R\) acts on vector \(v_0\) to generate \(v'\)

\[ \begin{align} v' &= Rv_0\\ &= \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 & 0\\ -1 & 0 & 0\\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -0.5\\ 1 \end{bmatrix}\\ &= \begin{bmatrix}-0.5\\-1\\1\end{bmatrix} \end{align} \]

items.title: Introduction
items.text:
Hand Sensory Rehabilitation for Stroke Patients: This project, motivated and advised by Dr. Sanford Meek, and Dr. Mohommed Sbai, culminated my bachelor's degree in Mechanical Engineering. In some stroke patients, the cortical pathways in the affected side of the body can become jumbled. From the perspective of the stroke patient, this means that physical stimuli located on the pinky finger might be perceived as occurring on the thumb, and vice-versa.

Over the span of two semesters, I worked in a group to understand the needs of potential users, and realized a wearable haptic device for sensory rehabilitation in stroke patients. The solution we created is intended to be used both in a clinical setting by a physical therapist and by the stroke patient themself at home.

The wearable portion of the device, which contains twenty vibrational motor-LED pairs, is applied to the affected hand, with operation controlled via a graphical user interface on a connected computer. Each vibrational motor-LED pair can be individually activated, or the pairs can be activated in groups (i.e., individual fingers, or the palm). Upon activation, the LED illuminates, and the vibrational motor vibrates (with pulse duration and intensity controlable). The therapist (or other user) can activate these vibrational motor-LED pairs in the fashion of a quiz, with the patient (hopefully) learning to correctly identify the location of the stimuli over time.

items.title: My Contributions
items.text:
Within this project, I championed the electrical design and created the initial Arduino software used to tune the device (it was later ported over to LabView to achieve the graphical user interface).

Control of the vibrational motor-LED pairs occurrs via multiplexing; that is, any individual motor-LED pair can be individually activated by energizing the corresponding voltage and ground connections. The graphic below gives an abstracted explanation.

Created using draw.io; see code on GitHub.

items.title: Design Day
items.text:
The Department of Mechanical Engineering holds a public event every semester called Design Day. At Design Day, any courses involving competitions are held, and the Senior Design groups present their projects via poster and any relevant physical demonstrations. For our demonstrations, we displayed the wearable haptic device on a 3D-printed hand, and allowed curious attendees to wear the device, and control it via the graphical user interface.

The Design Day poster explaining our project.

Group photo next to the Design Day poster; the group members left to right: Jordan Callus, Levi Barker, Jason Bermudez-Hernandez, Ethan Hawkins, and Melissa Frisby.

items.title: German Whispers
items.text:
In variant Sudoku, i.e., Sudoku with rules extending beyond the overlapping sets of 1-9, a popular rule that is used is called a German Whisper Line. On this line, typically colored green, adjacent digits along the line must differ in value by at least five. When I was first learning this rule, I found it very difficult to keep the options for each digit straight. So, I made this mathematical graph to remind myself of the rules. The nodes are the normal Sudoku digits, and edges are present between digits that could be adjacent on the German Whisper Line.

Made with draw.io.
